notes.b: Geographers can group a population by physical indicators (race) or by cultural indicators (ethnicity). The two ideas are easy to mix up, so keep them separate from the start.
points: Race: a grouping of people by inherited physical traits such as skin colour, hair type and facial features. It describes the body, not the way of life.
Ethnic group: a group that shares culture, ancestry, language, religion or history and is seen as distinct both by its members and by others. It describes shared culture, not appearance.
The syllabus treats race as one part of ethnicity, so race is one of several ethnic indicators. Language, religion and nationality (citizenship of a state) are the other cultural indicators.
notes.tip: Keep race (physical), ethnicity (cultural group) and nationality (citizenship of a state) as three separate terms. Irish Travellers are an ethnic group, not a race.

notes.b: Modern science has changed how race is understood. Biologists now see it as a weak way of dividing people, yet it still shapes the human map because people have acted on it.
points: All humans belong to one species, and people share about 99.9% of their DNA (the genetic code in every cell), so the differences between groups are tiny.
There is more genetic variation within any so-called race than between races, which is why the groupings do not mark real biological divisions.

Physical traits such as skin colour change gradually across space (these gradual changes are called clines) and have no sharp boundaries, so there is no point where one group clearly stops and another starts.
Race is therefore largely a social classification (one made by societies, not by biology)

It still matters geographically because people, laws and states have acted on it through segregation (forcing groups to live apart), apartheid (South Africa's system of legal racial separation) and genocide (the deliberate killing of a whole group of people).
notes.tip: Never suggest that any group is superior or that race decides ability or culture. Use neutral wording such as people of African descent.

notes.b: Older textbooks sorted humanity into four racial groupings. Biologists now reject this scheme, and it is presented here only as a historical, outdated classification.
points: Caucasoid: textbooks linked this grouping with lighter skin, straight or wavy hair and a narrow nose.
Mongoloid: textbooks linked this grouping with straight dark hair, an eyelid fold (epicanthic fold) and a broad face.
Negroid: textbooks linked this grouping with dark skin, tightly curled hair and a broad nose.
Australoid: textbooks linked this grouping with dark skin, wavy hair and a broad nose.
None of these traits makes one group superior to another, and the classification says nothing about ability or culture.
notes.tip: If you use these four names, present them as the traditional textbook classification, now rejected by biologists, not as science.

notes.b: Differences in appearance are not random. They built up as human populations adapted to the places they lived in.
points: Physical traits developed through adaptation to environment over thousands of years.

Skin pigmentation (melanin, the dark pigment in skin) increases towards the tropics, where ultraviolet radiation (the harmful part of sunlight) is strongest, so darker skin gives more protection there.
Lighter skin at high latitudes (places far from the equator) allows the body to make vitamin D from less sunlight, because skin needs sunlight to produce it.

notes.b: Before European colonisation (European powers taking over and settling other lands), and before about 1500, the main racial groupings were largely separated by oceans, deserts and mountains. This long isolation kept each grouping mostly in its own region.
points: Caucasoid peoples, such as Europeans, North Africans, Middle Eastern and South Asian peoples.
Mongoloid peoples: East Asians, Central Asians, the Inuit (the Arctic peoples) and the native peoples of the Americas.
Negroid peoples, such as the peoples of sub-Saharan Africa (Africa south of the Sahara Desert).
Australoid peoples: Aboriginal Australians and Melanesians (the peoples of the islands of Melanesia in the south-west Pacific).

notes.h: Colonisation of the Americas and the slave trade
notes.b: Colonialism (rule over other lands by a foreign power) and migration since 1500 overturned the old pattern, so most large countries are now multi-racial. The Americas show this most clearly.
points: Columbus reached the Americas in 1492. Disease (e.g. smallpox), war and forced labour caused the native population to collapse in the following century.

Spanish and Portuguese settlers produced racially mixed populations. Mestizo means European and Native American ancestry; mulatto means European and African ancestry. Mexico's population is mainly mestizo, so it is an example of racial mixing.
About 12.5 million Africans were shipped across the Atlantic as slaves between the 16th and 19th centuries.
Most went to Brazil and the Caribbean; far fewer went to the American South. Brazil received about 4-5 million Africans, more than any other country.
Brazil abolished slavery on 13 May 1888, the last country in the Americas to do so. The USA abolished it by the 13th Amendment (1865), after the Civil War (1861-65).
The legacy is large Black populations and racial inequality across the Americas, which is why the slave trade still shapes the region.
notes.tip: For the movement of people and racial patterns, give dated facts: the slave trade and colonial settlement in the Americas and Brazil, with the numbers above.

notes.h: Settler colonies: Australia and New Zealand
notes.b: In settler colonies, newcomers from Britain took over land where Indigenous peoples already lived. The result was lasting change to who lived there and how they were treated.
points: The First Fleet of British settlers and convicts arrived at Sydney Cove on 26 January 1788.
The Immigration Restriction Act 1901 began the White Australia Policy (a policy of keeping non-White immigrants out), which was dismantled between 1966 and 1973.
Stolen Generations: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children were removed from their families by governments, roughly from 1910 to the 1970s.
In the 1967 referendum (a national vote on one question) about 91% voted to count Aboriginal people in the census (the official population count) and let the federal government make laws for them.
Prime Minister Kevin Rudd made a national apology on 13 February 2008.
Census 2021 shows, for example, that about 3.2% of Australians identified as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander, and over a quarter of Australians were born overseas.
The Indigenous Voice to Parliament referendum of 14 October 2023 was rejected, with about 60% voting No.
New Zealand: the Treaty of Waitangi between the British Crown and Māori chiefs was signed on 6 February 1840. Māori are about one in six of New Zealand's population.
notes.tip: Australia is one of the settler examples to use for colonial settlement. Support it with dated facts such as the White Australia Policy, the Stolen Generations, the 2008 apology and the 2023 referendum.

notes.h: Removal of Native Americans in the USA
notes.b: The USA also moved its native peoples off their land. This changed where Native Americans live today.
points: The Indian Removal Act 1830 led to the forced removal of the Cherokee in 1838, known as the Trail of Tears.
Many Native Americans now live on reservations, a legacy of the removals (areas of land set aside for Native American peoples).

notes.b: When slavery ended, colonial planters still needed workers. Britain moved people within its own empire instead, which created new Indian communities far from India.
points: After slavery was abolished, Britain shipped indentured Indian labourers (workers bound by contract to work for a set period) to sugar colonies: to the Caribbean (Trinidad, Guyana), to Fiji (1879-1916), to Mauritius, and to Natal in South Africa (from 1860).
People of Indian descent are a large share of the population in Trinidad, Guyana, Fiji and Mauritius.
These movements created Indian communities in each destination, which is why Indian descent is common there.

notes.b: Colonial rulers did not only move people. They could also fix labels onto groups, and in Rwanda those labels later mattered terribly.
points: Belgium ruled Rwanda after the First World War.
From 1933 Belgian identity cards recorded each person as Hutu, Tutsi or Twa, so the labels became fixed and official.
The 1994 genocide, in which Hutu extremists killed mostly Tutsi, is set out in the racial conflict blocks below.

notes.b: After empires ended, migration reversed direction. People from former colonies moved to the colonial power (the mother country), which made European cities multi-racial.
points: After 1945 people from former colonies moved to the mother country. Caribbean and South Asian migrants came to Britain.
The Empire Windrush brought several hundred Caribbean migrants to Tilbury, near London, on 22 June 1948; post-war Caribbean migrants are known as the Windrush generation.
Later migration from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh also brought South Asian communities to Britain.
Algerians and other North and West Africans moved to France, and Indonesians and Surinamese moved to the Netherlands.
This migration created multi-racial European cities, because settled communities stayed and grew.
notes.tip: For post-colonial migration to Europe, name the UK and France with dated facts such as the Windrush of 1948.

notes.b: Migration within a country can also change its racial pattern. In the USA, a huge movement of African Americans changed two regions at once.
points: About 6 million African Americans moved from the rural South to cities of the North and West, such as Chicago, Detroit and New York, between about 1910 and 1970.
Segregation and poverty pushed them out of the South, and industrial jobs pulled them to northern and western cities.
The movement changed the racial make-up of both regions and created segregated inner-city neighbourhoods.

notes.h: Labour migration into Europe: guest workers
notes.b: Some European countries invited workers from abroad to fill jobs. Many of these workers stayed, which added new ethnic groups to the population.
points: West Germany signed a recruitment agreement with Turkey on 30 October 1961.
Guest workers (Gastarbeiter, the German word for them) were expected to return home, but many settled with their families, so Germany now has a large population of Turkish origin.
Belgium signed labour agreements with Morocco and Turkey in 1964.
North Africans also came to France and Belgium as labour migrants.
notes.tip: Guest workers are one of the expected topics for the movement of people and racial patterns. Use the Turkey and Germany dates.

notes.h: Refugees, asylum seekers and economic migrants
notes.b: People who move are not all moving for the same reason, and the law treats the groups differently. Learn the four terms and how they differ.
points: Refugee: a person outside their own country who cannot return because of a well-founded fear of persecution (serious mistreatment) based on race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership of a social group.
The 1951 UN Refugee Convention, with its 1967 Protocol, defines a refugee.
Asylum seeker: a person who has applied for refugee status and is waiting for a decision. An asylum seeker becomes a refugee only if the claim is accepted.
Economic migrant: a person who moves mainly for work or a better income.
Internally displaced person: a person forced from home who is still inside their own country.
UNHCR (the UN refugee agency) figures: over 120 million people were forcibly displaced worldwide in 2024.
notes.tip: A refugee, an asylum seeker and an economic migrant are not the same. An asylum seeker becomes a refugee only once the claim is accepted.

notes.b: The Syrian civil war is the main example of refugees changing the population of other countries, including in Europe.
points: The Syrian civil war from 2011 made over 6 million Syrians refugees, most of them in neighbouring countries.
Turkey hosted about 3.5 million of them, the largest number of any country.
In 2015 over 1 million refugees and migrants reached Europe across the Mediterranean, many travelling on to Germany.
Germany received about 1 million asylum seekers in 2015-16.
The Assad government (Syria's government during the war) fell on 8 December 2024, and some refugees began to return.
notes.tip: Refugees (Syria, 2015) are an expected example. Give the dated facts and the effects on the receiving society.

notes.b: The Rohingya show how losing citizenship can lead to mass flight.
points: The Rohingya are a Muslim minority in Myanmar, made stateless (belonging to no country as a citizen) by Myanmar's 1982 citizenship law.
From August 2017 over 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh, mostly to camps near Cox's Bazar.

notes.b: Ireland moved from a largely White, Irish, Catholic population to a multi-ethnic one. These are the figures to use for Ireland as the national example.
points: Census 2022: about 5.15 million people lived in Ireland, and about 20% (over 1 million) were born outside Ireland.
About 12% were non-Irish citizens, the largest groups being Polish and UK citizens.
About three-quarters described their ethnicity as White Irish, so about a quarter did not.
Polish is the most common language spoken at home after English and Irish, reflecting the large Polish-citizen group (Census 2016 and 2022).
Irish Travellers: about 33,000 people (Census 2022), under 1% of the population. The State formally recognised them as an ethnic minority on 1 March 2017.
Citizenship referendum, June 2004 (about 79% Yes): ended the automatic right to Irish citizenship for every child born in Ireland.
Ukrainians came to Ireland under the EU Temporary Protection Directive (an EU rule giving people fleeing war the right to stay), activated in March 2022 after Russia's invasion. Over 100,000 arrived.
notes.tip: Ireland's changing ethnic make-up is an expected topic. Use the Census 2022 figures and dates, and remember Irish Travellers are an ethnic group, not a race.

notes.b: Ireland's system for people seeking protection is part of the syllabus's national setting. Direct Provision and the right to work are the main points.
points: Direct Provision, which gives asylum seekers State accommodation and a weekly allowance while their claims are decided, began in 2000 and was widely criticised for long stays in shared centres.
A 2017 Supreme Court ruling found the total ban on asylum seekers working unconstitutional; from 2018 they gained a limited right to work.
More than 13,000 people applied for international protection (the formal term for asking for refugee status) in Ireland in each of 2022 and 2023.
notes.tip: Do not give a Direct Provision weekly allowance, a number of asylum centres or 2024-2026 application figures. These are not checked.

notes.h: Effects of migration on the receiving area
notes.b: Migrants change the place they move to, in ways that can help and in ways that can cause conflict. Keep your answer to the racial and ethnic pattern.
points: The population becomes more diverse, for example with new places of worship, shops and food.
Ethnic neighbourhoods form as migrants cluster near others from their own group.
Migrants supply labour to the receiving economy, so they fill jobs.
Discrimination, segregation and tension can follow. On 23 November 2023 a riot broke out in Dublin city centre after a stabbing on Parnell Square, fuelled by anti-immigrant agitation online.
notes.tip: For effects on the receiving society, give diversity, clustering and tension. Keep to the racial and ethnic pattern rather than general migration theory.

notes.h: Effects of migration on the source area
notes.b: The place migrants leave is changed too, in two ways.
points: The source area loses young adults, who are the most likely to migrate, so fewer workers are left.
Migrants send remittances, money that supports families who stay behind.

notes.b: A multi-racial society is one in which two or more racial groups make up significant shares of the population. Colonialism and migration have made this the normal pattern in large countries.
points: Examples include the USA, Brazil, South Africa, the UK and Ireland today.
Racial mixing, for example in Brazil: people of different racial backgrounds have children together, producing mixed-race populations.

notes.h: USA: melting pot or salad bowl
notes.b: The USA is a multi-racial society whose census shows growing Hispanic and mixed populations. Two images describe how its groups live together.
points: US Census 2020: White (alone) about 62%; Hispanic or Latino (of any race) about 19%; Black about 12%; Asian about 6%.
About 10% identified with two or more races, more than double the 2010 figure. Hispanics are the largest minority, so they make up about 19% of the population.
Melting pot: minority groups assimilate (adopt the majority's way of life) into one common national culture.
Salad bowl: groups keep distinct identities while sharing one nation.
notes.tip: Multi-racial societies expected in answers include the USA, with the Census 2020 composition and the melting pot against salad bowl contrast.

notes.b: Brazil is the main example of racial mixing in this option. Its population grew from three starting groups, then added later immigrants.
points: Brazil's population descends from Portuguese colonists, enslaved Africans and Indigenous peoples, with later Italian, German, Japanese and Arab immigrants.
Brazil has the largest Japanese-descended population outside Japan, mainly in São Paulo state, which shows the effect of later immigrants.
Census 2022: pardo (mixed race) about 45%, White (branco) about 44%, Black (preto) about 10%, Indigenous under 1%.
Census 2022 was the first census since 1991 in which pardo was the largest group, so mixed race is now the biggest category.
The ideal of racial democracy claims that mixing has removed racial division, but White Brazilians on average remain wealthier.
notes.tip: Racial democracy is a claim, not a fact. Do not say Brazil has no racism.

notes.b: The UK became multi-racial mainly through post-war migration from Commonwealth countries (former British colonies). Its census and the Windrush scandal show the result.
points: Census 2021 (England and Wales): White about 82%; Asian or Asian British about 9%; Black about 4%; Mixed about 3%.
The Windrush scandal (2018): some long-settled Caribbean-born residents were wrongly detained, denied services or deported because they lacked documents.
notes.tip: The UK is an expected multi-racial example. Pair the Census 2021 figures with the Windrush scandal.

notes.b: Governments can respond to diversity in different ways. Multiculturalism and assimilation are the two policy approaches you should be able to compare.
points: Multiculturalism: a policy of accepting and supporting distinct cultures within one society, as in Canada, which adopted an official multiculturalism policy in 1971, and Australia.
Assimilation: minorities adopt the majority culture. France's model expects integration into one secular French identity and does not collect ethnic statistics in its census.
Arguments for multiculturalism: enrichment, labour supply and tolerance.
Arguments against multiculturalism: segregation, parallel societies and backlash, including far-right politics.
notes.tip: Multiculturalism in the modern world is an exam topic. Give a definition, examples (Canada, Australia), benefits, problems, and the contrast with assimilation (France).

notes.b: Racial conflict (violent or serious conflict between racial or ethnic groups) has several causes.
points: Competition for jobs and housing.
Segregation, which separates groups and limits contact between them, so suspicion can grow.
Unequal power inherited from colonialism and slavery.
Racist ideologies, and fear of newcomers.
notes.tip: Northern Ireland, the Balkans and Israel-Palestine are religious or national conflicts, not racial ones. Do not use them as racial conflict examples.

notes.h: South Africa under apartheid, 1948-1994: the system
notes.b: South Africa is the main case study of racial conflict. Apartheid was a system of laws that separated people by race and gave power to the White minority.
points: Apartheid was introduced by the National Party after it won the 1948 election.
The Population Registration Act 1950 classified everyone as White, Black (African), Coloured (mixed race) or Indian/Asian.
The Group Areas Act 1950 assigned residential areas by race, so it enforced segregation.
Homelands, known as Bantustans, were set up for Black South Africans, so that Black South Africans were kept in separate areas.
District Six, Cape Town, was declared a White area in 1966. About 60,000 residents were forcibly removed and their homes bulldozed.
notes.tip: Apartheid is the racial conflict case drawn on in conflict essays. Give the four racial classes, the laws and District Six.

notes.h: South Africa: resistance, the end of apartheid and today
notes.b: Resistance and protest grew against apartheid and eventually ended it, but its effects have not disappeared.
points: Sharpeville, 21 March 1960: police killed 69 protesters, which shows the violence used against resistance.
Soweto uprising, 16 June 1976: students protested against being taught through Afrikaans (the language of many White South Africans).
Nelson Mandela was released on 11 February 1990 after 27 years in prison. The first all-race election, on 27 April 1994, made him President.
The Truth and Reconciliation Commission began work in 1996, so that the wrongs of apartheid could be faced.
South Africa Census 2022: Black African about 81%, Coloured about 8%, White about 7%, Indian/Asian about 3%.
Wealth and land ownership remain highly unequal by race, so the legacy of apartheid continues.

notes.h: The USA: segregation and the civil rights movement
notes.b: After slavery ended, the American South kept racial separation in law. The civil rights movement challenged it and won new laws, but tension has continued.
points: Jim Crow laws enforced segregation in the southern states after the Civil War.
Brown v Board of Education (1954): the Supreme Court ruled school segregation unconstitutional, so separate schools by race were not allowed.
The Montgomery bus boycott (1955) began after Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat.
The Civil Rights Act 1964 and the Voting Rights Act 1965 followed, because of the movement's pressure.
Martin Luther King, a leader of the civil rights movement, was assassinated on 4 April 1968.
George Floyd was killed by a Minneapolis police officer on 25 May 2020, leading to worldwide Black Lives Matter protests. The movement itself began in 2013.
notes.tip: US civil rights is drawn on in conflict essays. Cover slavery and the Civil War, Jim Crow segregation, the civil rights laws, and continuing tension such as George Floyd and Black Lives Matter.

notes.b: Nazi Germany shows racist ideology being turned into law and then into genocide.
points: The Nuremberg Laws (1935) stripped Jews of citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and other Germans.
Racist ideology was turned into law and then into genocide, so the Nuremberg Laws were a step towards the Holocaust.
About 6 million Jews were murdered in the Holocaust. Roma were also targeted for extermination.

notes.b: Rwanda is a genocide linked to the colonial labels described earlier, when Belgian identity cards fixed Hutu and Tutsi identities.
points: From 7 April 1994, Hutu extremists killed about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, in about 100 days.
notes.tip: Rwanda is drawn on in conflict essays. Link the genocide of Tutsi by Hutu extremists to the colonial classification on identity cards.

notes.b: Racial tension in Europe has also shown itself in riots in cities, in Britain and France.
points: Notting Hill, London, 1958, for example: white mobs attacked Caribbean residents.
Brixton, London, April 1981: clashes between mainly Black youths and police.
France, October-November 2005: riots spread through the suburbs (banlieues) of Paris and other cities after two teenagers died fleeing police in Clichy-sous-Bois. A state of emergency was declared.
Similar riots followed the police shooting of a teenager, Nahel Merzouk, in Nanterre in June 2023.
notes.tip: Riots are one of the problems to give when asked about multiculturalism. Use Notting Hill 1958, Brixton 1981 and the 2005 French riots.

keyTerms.definition: A grouping of people by inherited physical traits such as skin colour, hair type and facial features.
A group sharing culture, ancestry, language, religion or history that is seen as distinct by its members and by others.
A gradual change in a physical trait across space, with no sharp boundary between groups.
A society in which two or more racial groups make up significant shares of the population.
The having of children by people of different racial backgrounds, producing mixed-race populations.
A Latin American term for a person of European and Native American ancestry.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children removed from their families by Australian governments, roughly from 1910 to the 1970s.
Workers contracted to work for a fixed period, often far from home, as in the movement of Indian labourers to sugar colonies.
A migrant recruited for temporary work, such as a Gastarbeiter, who often settled permanently instead.
A person outside their own country who cannot return because of a well-founded fear of persecution.
A person who has applied for refugee status and is waiting for a decision.
A person who moves mainly for work or a better income, not because of persecution.
The Irish system of State accommodation for asylum seekers while their claims are decided, begun in 2000.
A model of assimilation in which minority groups merge into one common national culture.
A model in which minority groups keep distinct identities within one nation.
A policy of accepting and supporting distinct cultures within one society.
The South African system, 1948–1994, of legally classifying people by race and separating them in residence, education and public life.

questions.prompt: Examine the impact of colonialism and migration on racial patterns.
questions.model: (a) Colonisation of the Americas and the slave trade. Columbus reached the Americas in 1492, and disease such as smallpox, war and forced labour caused the native population to collapse in the following century. Spanish and Portuguese settlers produced mixed populations: mestizo (European and Native American) and mulatto (European and African) are Latin American terms, and Mexico's population is mainly mestizo. About 12.5 million Africans were shipped across the Atlantic as slaves between the 16th and 19th centuries, and Brazil received about 4–5 million, more than any other country. Brazil abolished slavery on 13 May 1888, the last country in the Americas to do so. Brazil's mixed population is shown by Census 2022, in which pardo (mixed race) was about 45%, the largest group for the first time since 1991, with White (branco) about 44% and Black (preto) about 10%. The ideal of racial democracy denies racial division, but White Brazilians on average remain wealthier. (b) Settler colonies. The First Fleet arrived at Sydney Cove on 26 January 1788. The Immigration Restriction Act 1901 began the White Australia Policy, which was dismantled between 1966 and 1973. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children were removed from their families under the Stolen Generations, roughly from 1910 to the 1970s. About 91% voted in the 1967 referendum to count Aboriginal people in the census, and Kevin Rudd apologised on 13 February 2008. In Census 2021 about 3.2% of Australians identified as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander, and over a quarter were born overseas. In New Zealand the Treaty of Waitangi between the Crown and Māori chiefs was signed on 6 February 1840, and Māori are about one in six of the population. (c) Post-colonial and guest-worker migration to Europe. After 1945 people from former colonies moved to Britain. The Empire Windrush brought several hundred Caribbean migrants to Tilbury on 22 June 1948, and migration from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh followed. Census 2021 for England and Wales recorded White about 82%, Asian or Asian British about 9%, Black about 4% and Mixed about 3%. West Germany recruited Turkish guest workers from 30 October 1961; many settled with their families, so Germany now has a large population of Turkish origin. (d) Refugees and Ireland's changing pattern. A refugee cannot return because of a well-founded fear of persecution, and an asylum seeker is waiting for a decision on that claim. The Syrian civil war from 2011 produced over 6 million refugees, and in 2015 over 1 million refugees and migrants reached Europe. In Ireland, Census 2022 found about 20% born outside Ireland and about three-quarters White Irish. Direct Provision, begun in 2000, housed asylum seekers, and over 100,000 Ukrainians came under the EU Temporary Protection Directive from March 2022.

questions.prompt: Racial conflict can occur in multi-racial societies. Discuss.
questions.model: Racial conflict arises from competition for jobs and housing, from segregation, from unequal power inherited from colonialism and slavery, from racist ideologies and from fear of newcomers. Apartheid South Africa is the main case study. Introduced by the National Party after the 1948 election, apartheid classified everyone as White, Black (African), Coloured (mixed race) or Indian/Asian under the Population Registration Act 1950, and the Group Areas Act 1950 assigned residential areas by race. Homelands, known as Bantustans, were set up for Black South Africans. In District Six, Cape Town, about 60,000 residents were forcibly removed after the area was declared a White area in 1966. Police killed 69 protesters at Sharpeville on 21 March 1960, and the Soweto uprising of 16 June 1976 protested against teaching through Afrikaans. Nelson Mandela was released on 11 February 1990 after 27 years in prison, and the first all-race election on 27 April 1994 made him President. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission began in 1996, but wealth and land ownership remain highly unequal by race. The USA shows the same causes at work through segregation: Jim Crow laws enforced segregation in the southern states after the Civil War; Brown v Board of Education (1954) ruled school segregation unconstitutional; the Montgomery bus boycott (1955) began after Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat; the Civil Rights Act 1964 and Voting Rights Act 1965 followed; and George Floyd's killing by a Minneapolis police officer on 25 May 2020 led to worldwide Black Lives Matter protests. Rwanda shows how a colonial classification could become fatal: Belgian identity cards from 1933 recorded Hutu, Tutsi or Twa, and from 7 April 1994 Hutu extremists killed about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, in about 100 days. Conflict therefore grows where a group is separated by residence, locked into unequal power and labelled by racist ideology, and these conditions in apartheid South Africa, the USA and Rwanda were the basis for violence.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a refugee and an asylum seeker, and describe one way Ireland has responded to asylum seekers.
questions.model: A refugee is a person outside their own country who cannot return because of a well-founded fear of persecution, as defined by the 1951 UN Refugee Convention. An asylum seeker has applied for refugee status and is waiting for a decision; they become a refugee only if the claim is accepted. Ireland responded by introducing Direct Provision in 2000, which provides State accommodation and a weekly allowance to asylum seekers while their claims are decided. It was widely criticised for long stays in shared centres. A 2017 Supreme Court ruling found the total ban on working unconstitutional, and from 2018 asylum seekers gained a limited right to work.
